title: Thrombin Time, Haemophilia A and B, Factor VIII, and Christmas Disease

steps.tx: The **thrombin clotting time** directly assesses the final step of the common coagulation pathway: the proteolytic cleavage of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin monomers. Exogenous bovine or human thrombin is added to citrated platelet-poor plasma, bypassing the intrinsic, extrinsic, and tenase complexes entirely (reference range fourteen to nineteen seconds). The thrombin time prolongs markedly in quantitative hypofibrinogenemia under one hundred milligrams per deciliter, qualitative dysfibrinogenemia, severe hyperfibrinogenolysis, or in the presence of therapeutic thrombin inhibitors including unfractionated heparin and dabigatran.
steps.say: The thrombin time measures the direct conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin by adding exogenous thrombin to citrated plasma. Because it bypasses both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, it tests only the final step of clot formation. The thrombin time is prolonged in hypofibrinogenemia, in qualitative dysfibrinogenemia, and in the presence of thrombin inhibitors like unfractionated heparin or direct oral thrombin inhibitors such as dabigatran.

steps.tx: When an unexpectedly prolonged thrombin time is encountered, performing a **reptilase time test** immediately clarifies whether the etiology represents heparin contamination versus a true fibrinogen abnormality. Reptilase, an enzyme isolated from the venom of Bothrops atrox, cleaves only fibrinopeptide A from fibrinogen. Because reptilase activity is completely independent of antithrombin III, it is entirely unaffected by therapeutic or catheter-flush heparin. A prolonged thrombin time paired with a normal reptilase time confirms heparin effect, whereas prolongation of both indicates afibrinogenemia or dysfibrinogenemia.
steps.say: The reptilase time is the definitive test to distinguish heparin contamination from a true fibrinogen defect. Reptilase is a snake venom enzyme that cleaves fibrinopeptide A to initiate clotting. Unlike thrombin, reptilase is completely insensitive to heparin and antithrombin three. If the thrombin time is prolonged but the reptilase time is completely normal, heparin contamination is confirmed. If both tests are prolonged, a genuine fibrinogen deficiency or abnormal dysfibrinogenemia is present.

steps.tx: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder resulting from loss-of-function mutations in the F8 gene located on chromosome Xq28, producing deficiency of **coagulation factor VIII**. Affecting one in five thousand live male births, it classically presents with spontaneous, painful, deep musculoskeletal bleeding episodes, predominantly recurrent hemarthroses into large hinge joints (knees, elbows, ankles) and extensive intramuscular haematomas. Laboratory testing demonstrates an isolated prolongation of the activated partial thromboplastin time that corrects on 1:1 mixing, with normal prothrombin time, normal bleeding time, and normal platelet counts.
steps.say: Haemophilia A is the classical X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by mutations in the factor eight gene. It almost exclusively affects males, presenting with deep musculoskeletal haemorrhages rather than superficial petechiae. Repeated spontaneous bleeding into large hinge joints like knees and ankles produces chronic crippling haemophilic arthropathy. Laboratory workup reveals an isolated prolongation of the APTT that corrects with normal plasma, while PT and platelet counts remain completely normal.

steps.tx: In circulation, factor VIII exists in an essential non-covalent stoichiometric complex with **von Willebrand factor carrier protein**. Von Willebrand factor protects factor VIII from rapid proteolytic inactivation by activated protein C and factor Xa, extending the intravascular half-life of factor VIII from two hours to twelve hours. Furthermore, von Willebrand factor delivers factor VIII directly to sites of vascular endothelial injury. Consequently, in severe type 3 von Willebrand disease, secondary deficiency of factor VIII develops due to accelerated clearance, leading to deep soft tissue bleeding mimicking classic haemophilia.
steps.say: Factor eight circulates in plasma tightly bound to von Willebrand factor. This carrier protein protects factor eight from premature proteolytic degradation by activated protein C, extending its half-life from two hours up to twelve hours. When von Willebrand factor is deficient, as in severe type three von Willebrand disease, unbound factor eight is cleared rapidly from circulation, causing secondary factor eight deficiency that can produce joint and muscle bleeding resembling classic haemophilia.

steps.tx: Clinical severity in both haemophilia A and haemophilia B correlates strictly with the measured **baseline factor activity level**. Severe haemophilia corresponds to less than one percent factor activity (less than 0.01 international units per milliliter), characterized by frequent spontaneous hemarthroses and life-threatening intracranial haemorrhages. Moderate haemophilia encompasses factor levels between one and five percent, with bleeding triggered by minor trauma. Mild haemophilia displays factor levels between five and forty percent, where patients experience prolonged haemorrhage only following major surgical procedures, dental extractions, or severe accidental trauma.
steps.say: The severity of haemophilia is strictly determined by baseline factor activity. Severe disease, defined by factor activity under one percent of normal, causes frequent spontaneous bleeding into joints and muscles without preceding injury. Moderate haemophilia, with activity between one and five percent, causes severe bleeding after minor trauma. Mild haemophilia, with five to forty percent activity, may go undiagnosed until prolonged bleeding follows major surgery or tooth extraction.

steps.tx: Haemophilia B, historically designated **Christmas disease**, is an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder caused by mutations in the F9 gene on chromosome Xq27, leading to quantitative deficiency or qualitative dysfunction of factor IX. Clinically indistinguishable from haemophilia A, it presents with identical joint hemarthroses, muscle haematomas, and prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. Factor IX is a vitamin K-dependent serine protease with a longer plasma half-life (eighteen to twenty-four hours) than factor VIII, requiring specific chromogenic or one-stage factor assays to definitively differentiate it from haemophilia A.
steps.say: Haemophilia B, or Christmas disease, is caused by mutations in the factor nine gene on the X chromosome. Clinically and through routine screening tests, haemophilia B is completely identical to haemophilia A: both produce spontaneous hemarthroses, deep haematomas, and an isolated prolonged APTT. The only way to tell them apart is by ordering specific factor eight and factor nine activity assays. Factor nine has a longer half-life of roughly twenty-four hours.

steps.tx: The management of haemophilia centers on prophylactic replacement of the deficient factor with recombinant or plasma-derived viral-inactivated concentrates. For patients with mild haemophilia A, **desmopressin acetate administration** induces transient two to four-fold increases in endogenous factor VIII and von Willebrand factor by stimulating exocytosis from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies. The major modern therapeutic complication in severe haemophilia is the development of neutralizing alloantibody inhibitors (measured in Bethesda units), occurring in twenty-five to thirty percent of severe haemophilia A patients following factor exposure.
steps.say: Modern haemophilia care relies on regular prophylactic infusions of recombinant factor eight or factor nine concentrates to keep trough levels above one to three percent. In mild haemophilia A, intravenous or intranasal desmopressin can be used to release stored factor eight from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies, avoiding blood products. The most serious treatment complication is the emergence of neutralizing IgG alloantibodies, called inhibitors, which occur in up to thirty percent of severe haemophilia A patients.

steps.tx: The introduction of **emicizumab bispecific antibody therapy** has transformed prophylaxis in haemophilia A. Emicizumab is a humanized bispecific monoclonal antibody engineered to simultaneously bind activated factor IXa with one arm and zymogen factor X with the other arm. By physically bridging these two enzymes in the proper spatial orientation, emicizumab mimics the cofactor function of activated factor VIIIa, restoring tenase complex activity. Administered subcutaneously once weekly or monthly, it effectively prevents bleeding even in patients who harbor high-titer neutralizing factor VIII inhibitors.
steps.say: Emicizumab is a groundbreaking bispecific monoclonal antibody that mimics the cofactor function of activated factor eight. One arm of the antibody binds factor nine-a while the other arm grasps factor ten, bringing them into close proximity on the cell membrane to activate factor ten. Because emicizumab has a completely different molecular structure from factor eight, it is not neutralized by factor eight inhibitors, providing reliable subcutaneous prophylaxis.

quiz.q: What coagulation test result distinguishes unfractionated heparin contamination from a true fibrinogen deficiency or dysfibrinogenemia?
options: Prolonged thrombin time with a completely normal reptilase time
Prolonged prothrombin time with a normal activated partial thromboplastin time
Shortened thrombin time that normalizes upon incubation with protamine
Complete correction of the bleeding time upon adding desmopressin
quiz.explain: Reptilase is insensitive to heparin and antithrombin III; therefore, heparin contamination causes a prolonged thrombin time with a normal reptilase time, while fibrinogen defects prolong both.

quiz.q: What is the typical laboratory coagulation profile observed in an uncomplicated patient with severe haemophilia A?
options: Isolated prolonged APTT with normal PT, normal platelet count, and normal bleeding time
Prolonged PT and prolonged APTT with severe thrombocytopenia
Isolated prolonged PT with normal APTT and elevated D-dimer
Normal PT and normal APTT with prolonged bleeding time and giant platelets
quiz.explain: Haemophilia A is an isolated deficiency of factor VIII in the intrinsic pathway, causing an isolated prolongation of the APTT while PT, platelet count, and bleeding time remain normal.

quiz.q: What factor activity threshold defines severe haemophilia A and haemophilia B?
options: Less than 1% of normal factor activity (<0.01 IU/mL)
Between 1% and 5% of normal factor activity
Between 5% and 40% of normal factor activity
Between 40% and 50% of normal factor activity
quiz.explain: Severe haemophilia is defined by baseline factor activity of less than 1% (<0.01 IU/mL), predisposing patients to spontaneous hemarthroses and muscle haematomas.
